title: Adaptive response tiling and SDK composer PRD (sketch)
content:
Summary:

This doc sketches a PRD for two linked capabilities: (1) an adaptive response tiling layer in the Hosted API that slices large or multipart model outputs into deterministic, resume-able tiles with structured metadata, and (2) an SDK Composer surface that exposes a composable, ergonomic client for stitching tiles, authoring tool-handshake contracts, and expressing fidelity tiers for clients with constrained latency/bandwidth. The goal is to improve developer ergonomics for large streaming responses and tool-calling workflows while keeping operational surface area small.

Background and problem:

Teams building chat assistants and extractive features often hit three friction points:
- Monolithic streaming payloads are brittle on unreliable networks (mobile, flaky corporate proxies). Long responses fail without a simple resume/partial-commit model.
- Tool-calling flows (search, DB reads, external APIs) need clear handshake and partial-commit primitives so clients can render partial results and retry sub-steps without forcing the model to re-run from scratch.
- Clients vary widely in their latency, memory, and bandwidth budgets. The current Hosted API supports streaming but leaves higher-level tiling, resume, and fidelity negotiation to each integrator, which increases integration complexity and inconsistent UX.

Goals (success metrics):

1) Developer ergonomics: Reduce lines-of-code for common resume-and-tool-call patterns by 50% in SDK-integrated examples.
2) Reliability: Increase successful end-to-end completion rates for long-form streaming sessions by 20% on flaky mobile networks (internal sim).
3) Latency/Fidelity tradeoffs: Enable clients to request a low-latency summary tile that captures >=85% of user-visible intent 70% of the time (measured via eval prompts).
4) Operational simplicity: No more than +10% increase in Hosted API p99 CPU usage for typical streaming traffic when tiles and metadata are enabled.

Non-goals:

- Not designing a new language for tool schemas. We will re-use existing typed-output primitives and JSON schemas where possible.
- Not replacing the existing streaming websocket/HTTP chunking primitives — this is an orthogonal, higher-level semantic layer implemented on top of streaming.

User personas and primary flows:

- Product Engineer (web): Needs resumable transcript tiles and a compact SDK method to fetch missing tiles and rehydrate UI while preserving model session context.
- Mobile Developer: Must minimize bytes over cellular; prefers coarse-grained low-fidelity tiles first then fetch higher-fidelity tiles on user demand.
- Solutions Engineer: Integrates tool calls with external systems and wants deterministic IDs and idempotency for tool-handshake frames.

Core features (high level):

A) Adaptive Response Tiling (server-side):
- Output tiles: The runtime can emit logical tiles (tile_id, seq_no, continuity_token, fidelity_hint, schema_hint, payload). Each tile is self-descriptive and can be applied incrementally to a client transcript.
- Resume tokens: Compact continuity_token values let clients request missing tiles or resume from a specific tile without full model re-run. Tokens encode minimal KV-cache checkpoint info or a pointer to server-side stored partial state (subject to retention policy).
- Fidelity hints: Tiles are annotated with fidelity_hint (e.g., minimal/summary/complete) to enable staged fetching.
- Tool call wireframes: Tool handshake frames are tiles that include call_id, expected_side_effects, and required_inputs. Tool sub-tiles allow partial tool results to be committed independently.

B) SDK Composer (client-side):
- High-level primitives: Composer.stream(session_opts) returns an object with: onTile(callback), requestTile(tile_id, fidelity), callTool(tool_spec, inputs, opts), and resumeFrom(token). The SDK manages backoff/retry and incremental state merging.
- Declarative composition: A light-weight DSL for declaring composite widgets: Example: composer.compose([tileBinder('summary'), toolBinder('search', {policy:'speculative'})])
- Offline reconciliation: The SDK caches tiles and can reconcile with server per a conflict resolution strategy (last-commit-wins or application-provided merge hooks).

API sketches (examples):

1) Streaming summary-first flow (pseudo):
- Client: POST /v1/sessions?tile_mode=adaptive&fidelity=summary
- Server: stream -> {tile_id: "t0", fidelity_hint: "summary", payload: {...}}
- Client displays t0 while SDK concurrently requests composition of full tiles if user scrolls.

2) Tool-call handshake (pseudo):
- Server emits tile: {type: "tool_handshake", call_id: "c42", tool: "search", schema: {...}, idempotency_key: "k-..."}
- SDK callTool returns promise; SDK attaches call results as committed tiles when tool returns.

SDK ergonomics notes (priorities):
- Minimal mental model: keep the public surface small and JS-first ergonomics with parity across Python/Go SDKs.
- Async-first: expose async iteration and event callbacks for streaming tiles.
- Declarative defaults: sensible default retry/backoff, tile retention, and fidelity fallbacks, but allow opt-outs for advanced integrators.
- Pluggable serializers: allow apps to map schema_hint -> deserializer hooks for typed tool outputs.

Telemetry and observability:
- New telemetry events: tile_emitted, tile_fetched, tile_resume_attempt, tool_handshake_emitted, tool_call_attempt, tool_call_commit.
- Include tile_latency, tile_size_bytes, continuity_token_age in logs.
- Rollup dashboards: tile success rate by fidelity, resume success rate by network type, p99 tile commit duration.

Security, retention, and operational constraints:
- Continuity tokens may reference ephemeral server-side checkpoints. Default retention: 24 hours, configurable on Dedicated/Private.
- Tool handshake tiles must propagate caller auth context; SDK will provide helpers to attach signed metadata for enterprise integrations.
- Size limits: tile payload default max 256KB; larger payloads force chunked tiling and explicit client rehydration calls.

Migration and rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (experiment): internal SDK-only experiment with a small set of integration partners; server tiles stored for 2 hours.
- Phase 1 (beta): expose HTTP headers to opt in to tiling; add JS SDK Composer with onTile and requestTile.
- Phase 2 (GA): enable tiling by default for long outputs; surface fidelity policy in console and per-route settings.

Open questions / risks:
- How large can continuity tokens be before they become unwieldy for clients? Can we rely on server-side checkpoint storage for most cases?
- Cost: storing partial session checkpoints increases storage burden and cross-tenant retention policy complexity.
- Eval: how to measure perceptual fidelity of summary tiles without a large labeling effort? Proposed: automated heuristics + small human-in-the-loop dataset.

Next steps (immediate):
- Engineering spike: runtime prototype emitting tiles for 3 common models (small, medium, long-context) using in-memory checkpoints. 2-week spike.
- SDK spike: JS composer prototype exposing onTile/resume/requestTile with a simple demo chat UI. 1-week spike.
- Product: draft console settings UI and per-route fidelity knobs; sample migration docs for customers.

Appendix: short demo scenarios and sample payloads (kept minimal here for readability).

-- end of sketch --
